assessmentSummary.identity: One exact Source 44 wall-supported bilateral flat-floor standing calf raise begins facing a stable wall with both hands in light continuous contact, both full feet planted about hip-width, and both knees mostly straight without forced locking. Press through both forefeet to raise both heels simultaneously through comfortable plantarflexion, reach a brief untimed top checkpoint, then lower both heels under control to the same full-foot floor contact. One complete rise-and-return cycle is one repetition. Stance width, small foot-angle changes, comfortable range, tempo, the brief non-dose checkpoint, breathing, repetitions, sets, rest, effort, footwear, and delivery context are annotations. Step range, unilateral or alternating action, unsupported balance, bent-knee delivery, external load, a sustained isometric hold, assisted-rise eccentric-only lowering, fast elastic action, locomotion, compound actions, clinical testing, or sport actions change the variant or definition.
currentCardFindings: Source 44 and the older Standing Calf Raise survivor describe the same standing plantarflexion family, while the current rows conflict on slug, support, laterality, start, return, count, and publication semantics. Sources 762, 841, and 1104 are contraction-mode variants, not independent movement definitions.

Earlier automated consolidation correctly preserved several aliases but over-broadened the selectable baseline to unilateral, loaded, isometric, and eccentric names without exact variant contracts. The new survivor keeps those names traceable while selecting only Source 44's supported bilateral flat-floor full cycle.

The inherited participant skill labels, age metadata, publication state, generic performance claims, and old difficulty values are not card-specific approvals. Difficulty is reassessed as exercise complexity and physical difficulty only; participant readiness remains a workout input.

Five YouTube candidates returned healthy oEmbed metadata. No candidate has been watched in full or approved for exact wall support, laterality, floor contact, rise, checkpoint, controlled return, count, captions, accessibility, cue quality, safety, or card-version match.
assessmentSummary.programmingDecision: Select only when the exact wall-supported bilateral flat-floor cycle, stable wall and nonslip level floor, suitable footwear, forefoot pressure, mostly-straight-knee posture, comfortable plantarflexion and controlled return, symptoms, restrictions, dose, duration, and cumulative calf, Achilles, foot, ankle, running, landing, jumping, cutting, and lower-body budgets fit. Do not silently change support, laterality, surface height, knee angle, contraction mode, return strategy, implement, load, count, elastic intent, compound action, or clinical scope. Recompute logistics, duration, fatigue, substitutions, persistence, and coach and athlete rendering after every change.

claims: A double-leg heel raise is a distinguishable bilateral plantarflexor task, and achieved heel height relates to plantarflexor activity in the studied protocol.

The exact Source 44 wall contact, flat-floor start and finish, simultaneous action, controlled return, count, and invalidation rules come from the legacy contract and Vortex specification rather than the study.
Standing heel raise includes distinguishable concentric rising and eccentric lowering phases across the lower-leg system.
The controlled taxonomy records a stationary braced standing task rather than misclassifying it as locomotion or impact.
Straight-knee heel raising recruits the triceps surae while foot position can alter center-of-pressure and measured activation.
The card records gastrocnemius, soleus, Achilles loading, foot stabilizers, joints, planes, and stabilization without promising isolated-muscle loading.
Concentric rising and eccentric lowering produce distinguishable activation patterns during standing heel raise.
Vortex specifies synchronized bilateral rise, a brief untimed checkpoint, and controlled return but does not infer an ideal universal height.
The bilateral heel raise deliberately loads plantarflexors more than ordinary walking in the studied comparison while remaining nonimpact and relatively low coordination.
The 22/32/32 proposal scores the exercise task only and remains queued for independent calibration.
Heel-raising and lowering configurations impose different Achilles loading and are not interchangeable.
Vortex tracks actual repetitions, active time, range, tempo, faults, symptoms, and overlapping lower-leg exposure; cumulative limits and recovery hours remain planning estimates.
Foot position changes center-of-pressure and muscle-activity observations, so stance and foot angle should be recorded rather than silently changed.
Stable wall support, a dry level nonslip floor, suitable footwear, comfortable forefoot pressure, and exact-task control are operational constraints, not demographic eligibility claims.
Resistance-training sets, repetitions, effort, rest, frequency, and progression should match the intended adaptation and individual response.
Prepare and capacity ranges are quarantined examples, not universal prescriptions, and end before height, timing, forefoot pressure, return control, breathing, or symptoms degrade.
A standing heel raise can be operationalized as a rising phase followed by a controlled lowering phase.
Vortex adds exact support contacts, bilateral timing, comfortable endpoint, brief non-dose checkpoint, same full-foot return, valid count, faults, and stop rules.
General resistance-training safeguards emphasize qualified instruction, safe equipment and environment, appropriate progression, and technique supervision.
No participant skill or age floor is inferred; symptoms, restrictions, exact-task control, environment, communication, cumulative load, and facility escalation policy govern selection.
Standing and seated calf-raise training are not interchangeable because knee position changes muscle-length and adaptation context.
The exact supported straight-knee task can serve preparation or capacity only when purpose and fatigue budgets fit; no universal transfer or outcome is promised.
Heel height is observable and relates to plantarflexor demand during double-leg heel raise.
Athlete support uses comfortable repeatable height, even forefoot pressure, synchronized rise, quiet return, breathing, and symptom checks rather than a maximal-height target.
Foot position materially affects observations and should be standardized when repetitions are compared.
Coaches record wall support, stance, foot angle, knee position, height, bilateral timing, return control, first fault, actual dose, symptoms, and downstream load without diagnosing.
Instruction, supervision, environment, and progression should fit the participant and exercise.

Written cues, visible counting, reduced comfortable range, fewer repetitions, more rest, captions, transcript, still images, or live instruction may preserve the exact task; changed support or action needs separate validation.
Support, laterality, rise assistance, lowering strategy, and exercise configuration change loading across heel-raise variants.
Step, unilateral, unsupported, loaded, isometric, eccentric-only, elastic, bent-knee, seated, compound, clinical, and sport tasks retain explicit variant or definition boundaries.
